newsitem.title: CAMBODIA: Cambodia's Ung Huot seen good fit for tough PM job.
newsitem.headline: Cambodia's Ung Huot seen good fit for tough PM job.

text.p: Cambodian Foreign Minister Ung Huot, the surprise choice to replace ousted First Prime Minister Prince Norodom Ranariddh, is known for an ability to court the goodwill of the international community.

Diplomats expect him to tap those talents right away in an attempt to polish the tarnished image of Second Prime Minister Hun Sen, who overthrew Ranariddh on July 6 following two days of fierce fighting in the capital Phnom Penh.
Hun Sen has since denied staging a coup and said he wants Ranariddh to be replaced, but the international community has yet to be fully convinced.
"He's an ideal choice because he'll polish Hun Sen's image, nothing more, nothing less. He's a great face for the government," one diplomat said.
But Ung Huot's task of persuading the world that Cambodia is on a democratic path looks tough and lengthy.

Reports of possible human rights violations, including a report that as many as 40 Cambodians had been killed for political reasons in the wake of Ranariddh's overthrow, could overshadow Cambodia's foreign relations for some time.
Diplomats said the decision to nominate the 52-year-old moderate reflects an understanding in Phnom Penh of how difficult it could be to regain international goodwill.
It will not be the first time Ung Huot has filled the shoes of a prince under controversial circumstances.
In October 1994 he took the post of foreign minister, replacing Prince Norodom Sirivudh who resigned to protest the ouster of opposition leader Sam Rainsy as minister of finance.
Ung Huot spent more than two decades in Australia where he received a masters degree in business administration at Melbourne University in 1974.
After finishing his studies, he decided not to return to Cambodia, where the Khmer Rouge, architects of the "killing fields" reign of terror, were about to take power.
He worked his way up the ranks of Telecom Australia over 17 years, from clerk to marketing executive, and in the 1980s began working for the royalist FUNCINPEC party in Australia.

In 1992 he returned to Cambodia to help lead FUNCINPEC to an election victory the following year and was elected to parliament. He became education minister under the new government and gained a reputation for integrity in the corrupt Cambodian school system where he tried to curb teacher bribes and exam cheating.
At the foreign ministry he distinguished himself by spearheading efforts to gain the country's entry into the Association of South East Asian Nations (ASEAN).
He now must win ASEAN over again after the grouping postponed Cambodia's membership following Ranariddh's overthrow.

"He's a realist, and some consider him compliant. His appointment will be generally welcomed as a positive development by ASEAN and the international community. He will play a good unifying and balancing role," said one ASEAN diplomat.

Ung Huot's nomination will be forwarded to the National Assembly when it reopens on July 28. Earlier on Wednesday, FUNCINPEC officials said they had agreed on Ung Huot's nomination for the first prime minister post.
Hun Sen's Cambodian People's Party would support Ung Huot's nomination in the National Assembly, an adviser to Hun Sen said.
